resources.string: About & privacy
ProxyFlow
Version %1$s · free, no account

ProxyFlow sends apps\' TCP connections to the proxy you choose. It doesn\'t make you anonymous: your proxy provider sees the sites you open, and apps and sites can still recognise you, for example when you sign in.
Privacy
No account, ads or analytics. ProxyFlow has no servers of its own.
Profiles stay on this phone. Usernames and passwords are encrypted with an Android Keystore key that is never exported or backed up. A password is only ever sent to the proxy it was saved for.
Your proxy provider can see which sites you visit and any unencrypted data.
What goes through your proxy

Websites and most apps use TCP, and their connections go through your proxy. Site names are looked up by your proxy, not by this phone. An app or Android\'s Private DNS that uses its own encrypted DNS goes through your proxy too, but then your proxy sees addresses instead of names.

UDP is blocked, so calls, some games and QUIC fall back to TCP or fail, and ping isn\'t answered. Devices on your local network, like printers, are reached through your proxy too, so usually not at all.
IPv6 addresses work only if your proxy supports IPv6. ProxyFlow answers names with IPv4 addresses only, and your proxy reaches the site however it can.

ProxyFlow\'s own connection to your proxy, the lookup of your proxy\'s name, and some traffic of Android itself and of its built-in apps, such as Google Play services, don\'t use the VPN. Nor do apps in a work profile, Private space or another user on this phone, or devices tethered to it.
TLS to the proxy encrypts the connection between this phone and your proxy. HTTPS sites stay encrypted end to end whether you use it or not: ProxyFlow never decrypts them.
ProxyFlow is free and independent. It isn\'t affiliated with any proxy provider.

Privacy policy
This policy describes ProxyFlow version %1$s.

ProxyFlow has no servers, no account, no ads and no analytics. What you enter stays on this phone, and ProxyFlow sends your traffic only to the proxy you choose. Your proxy provider, not ProxyFlow, can see the sites you open.
Kept on this phone

Your proxy profiles: their names, protocol, server address and port, TLS settings, whether they need a sign-in, and the result of the last connection test. They are in ProxyFlow\'s private storage, which other apps can\'t read.
Usernames and passwords, encrypted with AES-256-GCM under a key that Android\'s Keystore holds for each profile. The key never leaves the Keystore, and deleting a profile deletes its key.

A diagnostic log of connection events, error codes, counts and durations. It never includes passwords, server or site names, addresses or page content. It is kept for the time you choose in Settings (24 hours unless you change it), at most 5,000 events, and Clear removes it.

Your settings, which profile you chose, Android\'s system kill switch as Android last reported it, and, while connected, a note of the connection, so that ProxyFlow can tell you at its next start if Android stopped it.
None of this is included in backups or copied to a new phone. Uninstalling ProxyFlow deletes all of it.
Sent from this phone

While connected, apps\' TCP connections go to the proxy server in your profile, which connects them to the sites. Your proxy looks up the sites\' names and can see any data that isn\'t encrypted, such as pages that don\'t use HTTPS. Choose a provider you trust.
A profile\'s username and password are sent only to that profile\'s proxy. With TLS to the proxy they are encrypted; without it, anyone on the network between this phone and the proxy can read them.
If your proxy\'s address is a name, this phone looks it up through its usual DNS, outside the VPN.

Each time ProxyFlow connects or reconnects, including reconnecting by itself and switching to another proxy, and when you test a profile, ProxyFlow asks your proxy to open one connection to connectivitycheck.gstatic.com on port 443, a Google service, and closes it without sending anything through it. Google then sees a connection from your proxy\'s address.
ProxyFlow itself sends nothing to its developer, who has no servers to receive it: no usage data, crash reports or logs.
If you copy or export the log, you decide where it goes. It never includes passwords, server or site names, or addresses.
Android and Google

If your phone shares usage and diagnostics data with Google, Android may include ProxyFlow\'s crash and freeze (ANR) reports, and Google may show them to ProxyFlow\'s developer, with details such as the phone\'s model, its Android version, the app\'s version and the country or region the phone reported. ProxyFlow removes sign-in details, server and site names and addresses from the error messages it hands to Android, though Android writes the original message to the phone\'s own log, which other apps can\'t read.
Some traffic of Android itself and of its built-in apps, such as Google Play services, doesn\'t use the VPN, so it doesn\'t go through your proxy.
Permissions
VPN: Android asks you the first time you connect. It lets ProxyFlow send apps\' traffic to your proxy.
Internet and network state: to reach your proxy, and to notice when the phone changes network.
Foreground service: to keep the connection running while you use other apps.
Notifications (Android 13 and later, optional): for the connection status and its Disconnect button. Profile names are hidden on the lock screen.
Changes and contact
If a later version changes what ProxyFlow keeps or sends, its privacy policy will say so. ProxyFlow\'s developer can be reached through the contact details on its Google Play page.
Help
Getting started

You need a proxy from a provider, or a server of your own: an HTTP proxy that allows tunnels (CONNECT) or a SOCKS5 proxy, its server address and port, and its username and password if it has one. ProxyFlow doesn\'t sell or provide proxies.
In Profiles, tap Add proxy and enter those details. Test connection checks them without changing your phone\'s network.
On Home, tap Connect. The first time, Android asks you to allow ProxyFlow to set up a VPN: that is how apps\' connections reach your proxy. While connected, Android shows a key icon.
When something goes wrong
Home says what failed and what to try first, with a code such as AUTH_FAILED that Logs and your proxy provider can use.
Can\'t reach your proxy, or it isn\'t responding: check the server address and port, that your plan is active, and that your network allows the connection. Some networks block proxy ports.
Username or password rejected: check them with your provider. ProxyFlow supports the Basic sign-in of HTTP proxies and the username and password of SOCKS5, not Digest.
This doesn\'t look like a SOCKS5 or HTTP proxy: the protocol or the port in the profile is probably wrong.
Traffic blocked: while connected, ProxyFlow never sends traffic around your proxy. Try again, edit the profile, or choose Stop and use normal network.
Certificates and TLS to your proxy
TLS to the proxy encrypts the connection between this phone and your proxy, including your username and password. HTTPS sites stay encrypted end to end with or without it.

With TLS on, the proxy must present a certificate for the name in the profile, issued by an authority that Android trusts. ProxyFlow doesn\'t accept self-signed certificates, certificates you installed yourself, or any way to skip the check.

Certificate doesn\'t match: ask your provider which server name its certificate is for, and set it in the profile. Certificate not trusted, such as a self-signed one: ask your provider for a TLS address whose certificate is issued by an authority Android trusts. Certificate expired: check your phone\'s date and time first.
What goes through your proxy
Websites and most apps use TCP, which goes through your proxy, and your proxy looks up site names.

UDP is blocked, so calls and some games switch to TCP or don\'t work, and ping isn\'t answered. Printers and other devices on your local network are reached through your proxy too, so usually not at all.

ProxyFlow\'s own connection to your proxy and the lookup of your proxy\'s name, some of Android\'s own traffic, apps in a work profile, Private space or another user on this phone, and devices tethered to it don\'t use the VPN.
Kill switches
While connected, ProxyFlow holds traffic whenever your proxy isn\'t working: nothing goes around it. This is always on.

If Android stops ProxyFlow, or another VPN takes over, only Android\'s own setting keeps apps offline: Always-on VPN with Block connections without VPN. Only you can turn it on, in Android\'s VPN settings.
Set up the system kill switch
Logs and diagnostics

Logs list connection events and errors on this phone only, without passwords, server or site names, or addresses. Copy or Export passes them on when you ask your proxy provider for help. Settings has how long they are kept.
When Android stops ProxyFlow

To free memory, Android can stop ProxyFlow while it is connected; apps then use your normal network unless Android\'s system kill switch is on. ProxyFlow tells you on Home the next time it starts. It doesn\'t reconnect by itself; if it is your Always-on VPN, Android may start it again, or may not.
Getting help

ProxyFlow has no servers and collects nothing itself: what went wrong is in Logs, on this phone. Copy the log in Logs and include it when you contact your proxy provider, or ProxyFlow\'s developer through the contact details on its Google Play page.
